groundTruthNarrative: Copperleaf's roughly 17.6-minute ticket time outside Riverside is not inefficiency but the planned cost of its October 2024 made-to-order menu: the board accepted 4-5 extra minutes, every location rose by that amount that month with volume and headcount flat, and times have been stable since. Satisfaction, food quality, sales and average check are higher, and slower locations do not score worse. The 12-minute benchmark excludes scratch kitchens, and the 19.1 group figure is inflated by one location. A 2024 frozen-component trial damaged food quality, and a 2023 ticket-time bonus was gamed. The real problem is local: Riverside lost its saute/pasta cook in August, group operations deferred the GM's transfer requests, and the station bottleneck pushed ticket times to about 31 minutes. The GM's hours cut followed group labor policy; why the cook left is unresolved. Repeat visits rose with the redesign but also with a same-week rewards-app launch.

answers.rationale: The headline gap rests on a benchmark panel that excluded scratch kitchens and required 60%+ pre-prepared components (E3), and on a 19.1 group figure that falls to 17.6 without Riverside (E5). The remaining ticket time matches the 4-5 minute increase the board projected and accepted for the added scratch steps (E4), appeared at all locations in the launch month with flat covers and headcount, and has stayed within the board's 19-minute ceiling for two years (E5). Nothing shows kitchens slower than the menu requires, so the claim is contradicted, not merely unknown.

The board minutes document an explicit, quantified decision to accept about 18 minutes for made-to-order preparation (E4), and POS data shows the predicted step change in October 2024 at every location, with stable times since and no change in volume or staffing (E5). The 2024 trial shows that removing scratch steps shortens ticket time (E9), confirming that the preparation itself, not underperformance, drives the time.

Riverside's rise begins the month the saute/pasta cook left and the position stayed unfilled and uncovered (E10, E13, E15). The increase is concentrated on that station and is largest on nights it is worked by a trainee (E11). Covers fell slightly, and the other eight locations' times and ratings did not move (E5, E12). Wait-related reviews, comps and complaints rose at Riverside only (E12, E17).

Outside Riverside, overall satisfaction has been 4.6 every quarter since the redesign (up from 4.5). The speed attribute moved only from 4.2 to 4.1 and was already the lowest attribute before the redesign, so 'lowest-rated' (E2) does not show erosion. The slowest locations rank high on satisfaction (E6). Wait complaints are flat at 0.6-0.8% of tables, and the Harbour Road server's 'every night' is consistent with about one table per service out of about 140 (E16, E17). Same-store sales outperform the segment (E8). The only erosion is at Riverside, which is not group-wide.

A co-worker attributes the departure to the June hours cut (E14). The kitchen manager and GM report a family relocation (E13, E15). Scheduling records confirm the cut but show it applied equally to all four line cooks under a group labor standard, and three of them stayed (E10). No exit interview was done (E10). The operating partner's 'from what I hear' is hearsay (E1). Nothing in the evidence settles why he left.

Group line-cook turnover fell from 61% to 58%, no other location has had a line position open more than three weeks in 2026 (E10), and the other eight locations' ticket times and ratings are unchanged (E5, E12). The operating partner's 'that is what happens to the rest of the group' has no support.

The mechanism (added prep steps) and the size of the change were predicted in advance by a station time study (E4). The change happened at all nine locations in the launch month, with covers and headcount flat, which rules out volume and staffing as rivals (E5). The 2024 trial shows covariation in the reverse direction when scratch steps are removed (E9). Temporal order, mechanism, covariation and rivals ruled out together meet the causal standard.

The repeat-rate rise coincides with the redesign, and a parallel run of the old card-token method (38-39% vs 34%) shows the rise is not purely a measurement artifact, so the association is established and the answer is not 'unknown' (E7). But the Copperleaf Rewards app and its free-dessert sign-up offer launched the same week, a live co-intervention that could itself drive repeat visits, so causation is not established (E7).

The rise follows the departure date (E10). The mechanism is that the vacant station is the bottleneck (E13). 71% of the increase is on that station, and times scale with who covers it: the sous chef at weekday lunch versus a trainee on weekend dinners (E11). Rivals are ruled out: covers fell 2% (E11), and the other locations were unaffected over the same period (E5).

When ticket time rose about 4 minutes in October 2024, overall satisfaction rose rather than fell (E5, E6). Among the eight locations, the slowest ones rank second and fourth on satisfaction (E6). Complaints are flat (E17), and sales outperform the segment (E8). The evidence counts against the link.

The made-to-order positioning is the deliberate strategy (E4), and it underpins the premium check, food-quality gains and sales outperformance (E6, E8). A direct trial of frozen components cut food-quality scores from 4.4 to 3.9 for only a 1.9-minute gain, with guests comparing the food to a chain (E9). The 12-minute target is borrowed from non-scratch chains (E3). Group-wide adoption would likely worsen outcomes, and it would not address the one real problem at Riverside.

This action directly addresses the established cause (I9). The vacancy has gone unfilled for three months with no transfer despite the GM's two logged transfer requests (E10, E15). When the station is covered by an experienced cook, ticket time is close to baseline (E11). The losses are ongoing (E12), and the action is cheap and reversible.

This action corrects the client's mis-framing using the documented tradeoff and the invalid benchmark (E3, E4). It keeps a strategy whose results are positive (E6, E8). The baseline-plus-alert approach is what would have flagged Riverside in August (E5). It is among the best responses to the presenting request.

The June hours cut was applied to the whole line, as the group's own labor standard requires when covers fall, and Riverside's Sunday covers were 21% down (E10). The unfilled vacancy, the actual cause of the ticket-time rise (I9, E11), persisted because group operations deferred the GM's two logged transfer requests (E10, E13, E15). So even if H5 were confirmed, the GM would have followed group policy; replacing him would punish the wrong party for a group-level staffing decision and disrupt a location already in difficulty. The claim that he drove the cook out rests on hearsay (E1) and a disputed co-worker account (E14). Harmful, not premature: no confirmation of H5 would make this action right.

The group's own 2023 audit found that a ticket-time bonus produced KDS bumping of 18% of tickets and fake improvements with no guest benefit, and it recommended against this metric as an incentive (E18). A 12-minute target cannot be reached under the approved menu (E4, E5) without the shortcuts shown to hurt quality (E9). The action would corrupt the very metric that exposed the Riverside problem.

The evidence is sufficient to commit to substantive action: restore Riverside's staffing (causal link established, I9) and decline the group-wide frozen-component and bonus changes (tradeoff documented, harm shown by the trial and audit). The open questions, why the cook left (I5) and what drives repeat visits (I8), affect only the GM decision and attribution, not these interventions.
